- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped u
items.content:
Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety t
items.content:
New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

Read the full post on the Alignment Science Blog: https://t.co/24Gs1oSw7Q

items.content:
wildwood is a true marvel of human artistry, craftsmanship, and storytelling. i honestly found it even better than You Can See Everything (gasp!).

[spoilers if you read on]

an interesting trend in both wildwood and hoppers is how they handle death. they’re both movies for young people that treat death as inevitable and natural, and both expose the audience to a surprising amount of it. this feels quite different from the cleaner moral universes of much of modern disney and pixar.

both movies also have strong themes of non-intervention. of course, this is environmentally motivated, but there’s a broader Buddhist / Taoist morality running through both films: the world has a natural balance, and our attempts to impose our own ideas of goodness upon it can be destructive.

this feels quite different from the more Christian-inflected morality of overcoming evil. in these films, nature isn’t inherently good or evil, and trying to eliminate everything we perceive as bad can itself be the source of harm.

i wonder if this reflects a broader generational shift toward stories where it’s increasingly difficult to know what’s “right” or “wrong”, and where good intentions aren’t enough to make an action good.

both films feel like spiritual siblings to princess mononoke, questioning the hubris of humans who believe they can impose their will on the natural world.

wildwood is also visually spectacular and a complete and utter artistic achievement. it is always so rewarding to see fresh new takes on what a movie can be and how stories can be told.

huge fan, go see it!

"They're like, 'Okay, some really big company has a very specific problem... We're gonna spend two years building a very custom system to solve their problem.'"

"Chances are it won't work... doing product requires iteration. Even if it does work, who's to say that customer still has that problem? So boom, the company's done."

"Working with a diverse range of customers is this beautiful forcing function for building the right shape of product, which to us is a general robot."

"Most people have this mental picture of what the industrial base or manufacturing logistics looks like in the United States... You see these Rube Goldbergian machines of levers, and you don't see any humans in those pictures, right?"

"That's the top .01% of American manufacturing logistics. What's below that? You walk into these million square foot facilities and you see a bunch of people standing around on conveyor belts or folding tables doing things by hand."

items.content:
Deepseek just revealed every AI agent secret

Incredibly important article to read if you're building anything AI agent related

Here's basically everything you need to know about building a Grok Bot quality AI agent:

1. Agents are split between routers and workers. The user talks to the router, then gives the work to the workers. The router never does work. This is why the chief of staff model in Grok Bot works SO well

2. Proactive means acting on events, not chats. The agent should always be watching for events and react based on every event that comes through it. Routing to the right worker/action

3. Messages should be in a queue. Users should be able to send messages even while the agent is working, and each message queues/steers the agent

4. Besides the router and workers, there should be a watchdog layer. The watchdog makes sure the agent is always up and fixes it when there are issues. This is why Hermes succeeded and OpenClaw struggled. Constantly broke and couldn't fix itself

5. Protect human attention. Only message the user when it needs to act or the user can use the result. Lighten their cognitive load. Another thing Grok Bot is excellent at. When you message it you can be confident the next message you get will be it saying the task is complete.

Carve off an hour and read this incredible article

items.title: Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
items.content:
Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app Hey HN, we’re Wei-Wei and Jeff. We’re building Momentic, QA agents that autonomously plan, explore, and bug-bash controls and user flows in your web, iOS, Android, and (soon) desktop apps to catch bugs.

Here’s a demo: https://youtu.be/BFsM-Se1Fh8

We’re both software engineers that spent our careers on dev tooling and infra across companies like Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, and Qualtrics. Testing was always a pain in the ass (esp Playwright and Selenium), so we built agents to do it for us.

Modern day software has a ton of bugs and the change failure rate is only growing faster as coding agent adoption scales. LLMs are really good at generating code, but reinforce their own assumptions, write a ton of useless tests, and are bad at visual understanding. On DeepSWE v1.1, Sonnet 5.5 hit 66.2% pass rate when banned from writing tests, versus 65.3% when allowed.

OSS end-to-end testing frameworks like Playwright, Selenium, or Maestro force you to hardcode implementation details like XPath, text, or aria-* attributes in your tests. Even with agents, these take a nontrivial amount of time and tokens to build and maintain.

In 2023, we saw Nat Friedman drive a browser with GPT-3 via natbot. We were inspired to use this technology to automate the most painful and tedious parts of software engineering: testing. We started with using LLMs to generate and maintain Playwright, but quickly realized that those primitives were fundamentally misaligned with the agentic SDLC. We think the future of QA is agents testing themselves, not writing scripts.

Mo is a custom agent harness for catching bugs that builds on the past 3 years of Momentic and millions of test traces from complex, real-world applications. Mo is built for recall: it finds the most real bugs, though Codex is a bit more precise at 86% vs 84%. The tradeoff is cost: Mo costs $2.67 per bug vs $0.80 for Codex, less than Claude Code and Devin.

- Self-organizing agent graph. Mo builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) as it explores. Large product areas automatically fork into parallel sub-agents, each with their own browser or device for concurrent execution.

- Specialized agents for domain specific tasks. Planner agents reason over screenshots and video while dedicated locator agents inspect page structure to resolve plain-English interaction targets. Others include image analysis, video understanding, audio generation, and more.

- Parallel agents coordinate through cooperative resource leases. Agents can announce that they’re “using” or “modifying” overlapping resources or fixtures. Multiple “using” claims can coexist, but only a single “modifying” claim can be active on any particular one.

- Scaled infrastructure. Mo ships with a tunnel that lets users expose private sites and local apps to our hosted agents and infra. A single bug bash can spin up 100s of concurrent browsers and devices.

We benchmarked Mo against coding agents on 4 popular open-source apps: Gitea (58.8k stars), Metabase, Twenty (YC), and Saleor, with 1,396 human-labeled bugs. Each agent got the same brief, a fresh E2B sandbox, and no access to source code. Codex and Claude Code used hosted Browserbase browsers, while Devin used its built-in browser. For evaluators, we implemented LLM as a judge (GPT-6.1 Sol) with a human reviewer.

Results from a time-boxed 60-minute run:

- Mo: 269 bugs, 19.3% recall, 84% precision, $2.67 per bug

- Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol + Playwright MCP): 86 bugs, 6.2% recall, 86% precision, $0.80 per bug

- Claude Code (Opus 5.5 + Playwright MCP): 59 bugs, 4.2% recall, 80% precision, $4.09 per bug

- Devin: 27 bugs, 1.9% recall, 84% precision, $3.89 per bug

Mo finds more bugs the more time it has. From 30 to 60 minutes, it went from 177 to 269 bugs (+52%), while Codex gained only 16%.

Results: https://momentic.ai/qa-bench

Write-up: https://momentic.ai/blog/qa-bench

Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/momentic/qa-bench

Harness: https://github.com/momentic-ai/qa-bench

We just shipped PR testing for Vercel and Cloudflare deploy previews and we’re giving every new signup $250 in Mo spend. Paid plans have higher infra capacity and included usage along with options to top up.

We’d love for you to try it out and give us feedback. Feel free to comment here, we’ll be around all day!

We still haven't seen the limit of proactive AI. Not even close. 

Example: our video system went down for a few hours. We were emailing with our video provider to get them back up. When an email came through from that provider saying the videos were restored, my Dots:

(1) saw the email
(2) wanted to "help" me 
(3) logged into our video system with my credentials
(4) verified playback on all videos
(5) pinged me saying the playback worked and drafted my reply 

It means that now when an action seems out of place, I have to ping my team *and* I have to check my AI assistant history.

items.title: It's hard to believe that an AI freak like me uses less AI than ever before. Here are the only 4 apps I open (every day)
items.content:
It's hard to believe that an AI freak like me uses less AI than ever before. Here are the only 4 apps I open (every day):

> Claude (and Claude Code)
> Slack, to talk to my team
> Wispr Flow, for meeting notes & voice dictation
> Viktor, our AI employee in Slack

Viktor is on the list because he fixes the one thing that annoyed me about Claude:

Claude is only between me and the AI. I can’t bring/loop my team into the conversation.

As crazy as it sounds, I officially hired Viktor and added him to my team Slack. 

Now my team & I talk to each other in Slack, and Viktor collaborates with the entire team, using both Anisha’s Claude and mine (+ connected to all our apps).

Here’s what that looked like (watch the video):

1. I asked Anisha to turn my latest newsletter, “Claude for legal,” into a LinkedIn post.
2. Anisha sent a Slack message tagging @Viktor to build a page in Claude Code with prompts from the article.
3. Viktor replied with a live page link (in 2 mins).
4. I jumped in: I think we should do it differently.
5. Viktor started working with both of us in thread.
6. He went to my Substack, pulled the content, and built a lead magnet. Replied “Done” with a link.

This is what I wanted out of Claude Tag, a proactive collaboration. But it has too many bugs, so I hired Viktor instead.

How to set it up for your team:

1. Go to viktor .com & add it to your Slack (works in Microsoft Teams too).
2. Connect the tools you want it to use. I added the Claude API, for him to build in Claude Code.
3. Tag @Viktor in a channel with any task, written the way you’d message a team member.
4. Correct it in the thread when something’s off.

AI can now write, edit, and optimize code.

Anyone can use AI to build powerful apps.

But there are different kinds of AI coding tools.

► Some help non-developers build apps
► Others help existing developers build faster

It can be difficult to select the right tool and approach.

Here’s a complete guide to understand the differences:

1️⃣ Vibe Coding (Level: Beginner)

Think of this as building without traditional coding. You describe the idea in plain English, and the AI generates the functional application.

➟ When to use: Use this to test product ideas or build demos to show others.
➟ When to avoid: Do not use this for mission-critical production systems.
➟ ROI: Prove your product's value before spending your budget.
➟ Tools: Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Figma Make.

2️⃣ AI-Assisted Coding (Level: Intermediate)

This is developer-led work with AI accelerating the process. You write the code. AI provides real-time suggestions, fixes, and completions.

➟ When to use: Use this for your daily development work and to handle repetitive tasks.
➟ ROI: This can boost a developer’s productivity by 20-25%.
➟ Tools: GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Google Antigravity.

3️⃣ Agentic Coding (Level: Advanced)

This is when the AI handles complex tasks independently. You define the outcome you want, and the AI agent plans, codes, and tests the solution in a continuous loop.

➟ When to use: Ideal for modernizing legacy systems or making large-scale codebase updates.
➟ When to avoid: Don’t use this if the desired outcome is vague or poorly defined.
➟ ROI: It can be 2x faster for large-scale updates and legacy work.
➟ Tools: OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI.

There’s no single “best” way to use AI coding.

Each approach serves a different purpose.

Vibe Coding → Validate ideas before committing.
AI-Assisted → Increase team output.
Agentic → Automate complex, defined work.

items.content:
Harness engineering is the most f*cking DANGEROUS and accessible thing I've ever seen

engineers opened up the source code of 11 real coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenHands, Aider, Hermes) 

their answer: agent = model + harness

the harness is everything around the model. and every system they studied is built from the same 7 parts:

→  agent loop: the heartbeat. think, act, check the result, repeat until done or stopped
→  LLM integration: the bridge that talks to the model and reads its tool calls
→  tools & actions: what the agent can actually touch. files, code, the terminal
→  memory & context: what it remembers, what it loads, and what it compresses when the window fills up
→  safety & permissions: what runs freely, what asks you first, what gets blocked
→ orchestration: sub-agents that split big jobs. the smallest harness skips it entirely
→  extensibility: hooks, skills, plugins and MCP to add power without rewriting the core

what surprised them:

> across ~4 million lines of code, not one agent runtime imports LangChain, LangGraph or AutoGen
> none of them use vector search to find code. it's ripgrep, globs and markdown files
> skills (SKILL.md) are now in more systems than MCP: 9 of 11 vs 8 of 11

the best part for builders: 18 design recommendations and a 90-line starter harness that covers 10 of them

90 lines. that's the whole entry ticket

horror game in 4 days with claude opus 5.5 + godot..

pinterest references inspired by silent hill and fatal frame

the trick is code for the big stuff, batches for the small stuff. here’s the workflow:

- step 1: collect pinterest references for the mood and give them to opus
- step 2: run opus in auto mode: it edits files, runs scripts, launches godot, takes screenshots and keeps iterating
- step 3: buildings and big structures get built directly in code
- step 4: opus writes prompts for groups of 10 related props, and nano banana makes one reference image per group
- step 5: each image goes into meshy t2.5 (image-to-3d, smart topology) and comes back as a textured batch
- step 6: split the batches in blender by hand to save claude usage, then opus places them by location
- step 7: textures: nano banana makes 2x2 grids, opus crops them into 4 images, normal and roughness come from the color, and triplanar mapping means no uv unwrapping
- step 8: grime: opus places dirt decals along walls and corners and bakes ao into the props

the numbers:

> ~4 days, and the environment looked close to final by day 2
> ~10 batches = ~100 props
> claude pro plan, ~$90 api-equivalent for the core, ~$180 with experiments

generate props in groups of 10 that share one material. fewer credits, and everything matches (dev: One_Cheek_8843)

items.content:
Any excellent book to learn LLM Optimization and Serving

Why is it important to learn LLM Optimization?

Large language models (LLMs) are the reasoning engines of modern AI.

Without proper optimization, however, LLMs can be expensive and slow to serve.

So, it is necessary for any one (A/ML Engineers, Data Scientist) working on LLMs or LLM applications to be familiar with LLM optimization and serving techniques.

Hands-On LLM Serving and Optimization Book

This book serves as a comprehensive guide to the complexities of deploying and optimizing LLMs at scale.

This book covers

Chapter 1 — Introduction to Model Serving and Optimization: Anatomy of a model, the model lifecycle, what model serving is and why we optimize it, serving paradigms (edge, single-model, multi-model), and serving platforms.

Chapter 2 — Large Language Model Serving: Inside the transformer, autoregressive generation, decoder-only architecture, attention, the KV cache, prefill and decode, and running LLMs with a serving framework (vLLM).

Chapter 3 — Model-Serving System Design: A Deep Dive: Building online single-model and multi-model serving services from scratch, batching and streaming, NVIDIA Triton, and cost- vs. latency-optimized designs.

Chapter 4 — Model Serving Best Practices: Serving in an agentic world (agents, RAG, CAG), enterprise serving architecture, building with an open source stack or a cloud vendor, build-or-buy strategy, and performance measurement.

Chapter 5 — Challenges When Serving LLMs: Why optimization matters, accelerator chips and GPU specs, model-loading bottlenecks, KV cache sizing, and arithmetic-intensity analysis of prefill and decode.

Chapter 6 — Essential LLM Optimization Techniques: Request batching and scheduling (dynamic, continuous, chunked prefill), scalable attention and kernel fusion, model compression (quantization, distillation, pruning), and prefix caching / RadixAttention.

Chapter 7 — Advanced LLM Optimization Techniques: Speculative decoding, multi-GPU and multinode inference (data/tensor/pipeline/expert parallelism), prefill–decode disaggregation, and advanced KV caching for long-context serving.

Chapter 8 — LLM Serving Frameworks: vLLM internals (architecture, scheduler, layered optimization), TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, and how to select the right framework.

Chapter 9 — LLM Optimization in Practice: A step-by-step optimization plan for Qwen3-14B with vLLM, from hardware inspection and benchmarking to quantization, distributed serving, and common trade-offs.

Chapter 10 — Advancements in LLM Serving: Semantic caching, performance profiling, multimodal serving, edge AI, multi-LoRA serving, and model serving in reinforcement learning.
